Set up a conversion factor so the unwanted unit cancels and the desired unit remains. Then calculate the answer and round it to the same number of significant figures as the original measured value.

The last digit of a measurement is estimated, so calculated answers cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement. For addition and subtraction, the final answer is rounded to the same number of decimal places as the measurement with the fewest decimal places. To precision-correct a calculation, first find the unrounded total using a calculator, identify the measurement with the fewest decimal places, and then round the total to match that number of decimal places.

Significant figures show the precision of a measurement. They apply to measured values, not exact counts. All nonzero digits are significant, as are zeros between nonzero digits. Leading zeros are not significant, and trailing zeros are significant only when a decimal point is present. Scientific notation is a clear way to show the correct number of significant figures.

You should always estimate one digit beyond the smallest marked division. Every measurement includes some uncertainty because the last digit is estimated, and more precise tools reduce that uncertainty.

Scientific notation is a short way to write very large or very small numbers using powers of 10. A positive exponent moves the decimal to the right, and a negative exponent moves it to the left. A number in scientific notation has a coefficient between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10. On a calculator, the EE or E button represents “times 10 to the power of” and helps avoid errors.

In the English system, units for length, volume, and mass are not related. In the metric system, these units are connected. The meter is the base unit of length, the liter is the unit of volume, and the kilogram is the base unit of mass. One cubic centimeter of water equals one milliliter and has a mass of one gram, which shows how the metric system links volume and mass.

Early measurement systems used body parts, which made converting between units very difficult. The French developed the metric system to create a consistent standard, using the meter as the base unit of length. Metric units change by powers of 10, which makes conversions simple. Smaller units are made by dividing by 10, and larger units are made by multiplying by 10.
